full_text:
Jackson and Henry form a formidable rushing duo. Jess Rapfogel / Getty Images
Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.” And quoth Ronnie the Ravens fan, “ Yeouuugh! ”
Baltimore’s black-and-purple paladins have been quite successful since the turn of the century, with two Super Bowl triumphs and eight division titles to their name. The team is favored to win the AFC North again in 2026, thanks to an inspired series of offseason shake-ups.
Jesse Minter becomes the Ravens’ first new head coach in almost two decades. Declan Doyle takes over as offensive coordinator, while Anthony Weaver now oversees the defense. And the front office went all in by adding star edge rusher Maxx Crosby Trey Hendrickson, who has at least 13 1/2 sacks in four of the last six years.
Some All-Pro constants remain. Two-time MVP Lamar Jackson looks to bounce back under center in good health. Active rushing leader Derrick Henry has averaged a wild 5.6 yards per carry with Baltimore. Linebacker Roquan Smith and safety Kyle Hamilton are still standard-setters at their positions. Expectations are high, and for good reason.
Check out the schedule below, with information on how to watch both local and national TV games. The Ravens visit Rio de Janeiro to face the Dallas Cowboys in Week 3. They’re also lined up for four primetime games from Week 5 onward. Follow the team on The Athletic, and keep up with reporter Jeff Zrebiec — he’s the Ed Reed of Baltimore beat writers.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC, and it’s where you can find the Ravens’ first four games, including their showdown with the Cowboys in Brazil. The network’s theme music is also a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .

Playoffs: 1 wild-card game

The Ravens are currently set to appear in the final TNF game of the regular season, which pits them against the Cincinnati Bengals on New Year’s Eve.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.

full_text:
Quarterback Joe Fagnano (right) made the Ravens' initial 53-man roster as an undrafted free agent. Mitch Stringer / Imagn Images
With a new coaching staff and fancy new uniforms, the Baltimore Ravens have billed this season as the start of a new era for an organization steeped in stability, so it was fitting that general manager Eric DeCosta somewhat broke away from previous trends and tendencies in cutting his roster to the requisite 53 players by Sunday’s deadline.
Rather than doing most of the moves right up against the deadline, which is how they’ve done business in recent years because they believed the late activity gave them a better chance of getting more players through waivers, the Ravens knocked out all but a handful of decisions 24 hours beforehand.
The Ravens never like cutting rookie draft picks. However, among their 37 moves this weekend were the cuts of two rookie seventh-round selections: defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny and guard Evan Beerntsen. Neither got much traction in a preseason roster push.
DeCosta also abhors moving on from early-to-mid-round draft picks, but that didn’t save outside linebacker Adisa Isaac, a 2024 third-round pick who was limited to just four games in two seasons because of injuries. Isaac, despite a sack and flashes of potential in the preseason finale, was one of the team’s final roster cuts.
Baltimore’s decision-makers have rarely believed keeping three quarterbacks to start the season was a good use of roster space. They had done it just once over the previous five years. On Sunday, ex-Maine and UConn undrafted quarterback Joe Fagnano became arguably the most unlikely member of the 53-man roster as he earned a spot behind Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley, thanks to a preseason in which he completed nearly 75 percent of his attempts, threw for 509 yards and had three touchdown passes.
Fagnano wasn’t initially part of the Ravens’ undrafted class. He was planning to attend their rookie minicamp on a tryout basis, but the Ravens officially signed him and Heisman finalist Diego Pavia on the eve of the workout. Fagnano outlasted Pavia and then was one of the top-performing passers in the preseason despite getting limited practice reps.
“Coming into the situation, I knew what it was,” Fagnano said after Baltimore’s preseason finale. “I knew, just talking to people, how reps get distributed. I kind of knew coming in it was going to be an uphill slope. Just taking those reps behind (the QBs) in the walk-throughs, just getting as many mental reps as I can, staying locked in (and) knowing that, if my opportunity came, that I was going to want to make the most of it.”
Fagnano was part of the continuation of certain trends, too. For the 22nd time in the past 23 years, the Ravens kept at least one rookie undrafted free agent on the initial 53-man roster. Not only did Fagnano make the team, but so did Ethan Burke, an edge rusher out of the University of Texas. He parlayed a strong preseason into a roster spot, edging Isaac out for the No. 5 outside linebacker role.
“One thing I know is just keep working hard and doing what I do and consistently chasing getting better and (being) great,” Burke said last week.
DeCosta continued his habit of trying to add to his draft capital whenever possible. He turned two players who weren’t expected to make the team, nose tackle C.J. Okoye and undrafted rookie offensive tackle Diego Pounds, into draft picks. Okoye secured a 2028 seventh-round pick from John Harbaugh’s New York Giants, and Pounds went to the Kansas City Chiefs for a conditional 2028 sixth-rounder.
DeCosta also stuck to his preferred 25 offensive, 25 defensive and three specialists roster breakdown. That seemed in doubt when it was revealed that Fagnano had made the team and Baltimore was going with three quarterbacks, but starting rookie running back Adam Randall on temporary injured reserve allowed the Ravens to maintain that balance.
The Ravens, who relied largely on their back-end roster depth to go 3-0 in the preseason and outscore the opposition 78-13, knew they would lose some talent. They’ll learn Monday just how much talent they lost when the first wave of waiver claims goes through.
They’re surely hoping a number of their cuts clear waivers and return to their 16-man practice squad. Benny, Isaac, cornerback Robert Longerbeam, offensive tackle Gerad Lichtenhan and outside linebacker Kaimon Rucker are among the Ravens who could garner interest from other teams.
Overall, though, there wasn’t anything about the Ravens’ weekend moves that could be characterized as significant surprises. They’ve been a reasonably healthy team all summer, meaning the precious few available roster spots mostly accounted for depth and special teams considerations.
They had decisions to make regarding defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike and inside linebacker Teddye Buchanan, and they opted to keep both on the 53-man roster rather than move them to injured reserve and give them more time to return from neck and knee surgeries, respectively.
That doesn’t necessarily mean either will be ready for the Sept. 13 regular-season opener at the Indianapolis Colts. But it does allow them to keep participating in practice and accelerating their return. If the Ravens had put Madubuike and Buchanan, two projected starters, on IR, they wouldn’t have been eligible to practice through the first four weeks of the season. That would have been a significant setback for two guys working their way back from major injuries.
The Ravens did start cornerback Bilhal Kone on IR, which gives him time to recover from a late-preseason injury. He’ll be eligible to return as early as Week 5. The same goes for Randall, who was held out of the team’s second preseason game because of an undisclosed injury.
Everything else, though, from a typically dizzying day around the league, stayed true to form. With Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Devontez Walker, LaJohntay Wester and rookies Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt, the Ravens were essentially set at wide receiver when training camp began. That was also the case at tight end, with drafted rookies Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas joining veterans Mark Andrews and Durham Smythe.
When center Danny Pinter sustained a season-ending knee injury during joint practices against the Minnesota Vikings, that all but ensured the Ravens would go with nine offensive linemen. The only question was who would get that final spot, and that became close to a formality when veteran guard Andrew Vorhees, a 17-game starter last season, accepted a pay alteration during training camp.
Defensively, the decision to roster Madubuike and Buchanan eliminated most of the drama. The final interior defensive line spot essentially came down to Aeneas Peebles, Benny and Okoye. Peebles, who brings some diversity to the group with his pass-rushing ability, earned the job.
Inside linebacker Jay Higgins had another solid training camp, but the number of injuries the Ravens experienced at the position essentially left him unopposed for the fourth linebacker spot.

“The Athletic Football Show” is previewing all 32 teams leading up to the start of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Carolina Panthers. The quotes are edited for clarity. You can watch the whole preview on YouTube and in the embedded video below, or listen to the full NFC South preview wherever you get your podcasts.
Robert Mays on what about the Panthers most excites him: The Tetairoa McMillan-Jalen Coker pairing. I think it’s a good tandem of one and two receivers. I think Coker is a good NFL receiver. Stylistically, you can move them both around. They’re big enough where you can have them play a variety of roles. They’re kind of interchangeable. Coker is a willing and capable blocker if you want to use him on some of the insert stuff. He’s a tough, rugged player. McMillan had such a great rookie year.
Even if the offensive line is shifting and there’s other stuff we could talk about with the offense, those two guys being on the field for a majority of the snaps together this year in a way they weren’t last year (is big). They couldn’t use McMillan the way they wanted to last season because Coker wasn’t on the field for the first half of the year. They need Coker to be there for them to move McMillan into the slot and do all the things that they’re talking about. Coker is the guy that, in theory, can unlock McMillan in the ways that they want to. And so a full season of those two guys, that’s what I want to watch.
Robert Mays on what he’s watching the first month of the season: Is Jaelan Phillips enough to take that pass rush from a team that finished 32nd when rushing four to a unit that feels dangerous? Because that’s about more than individual talent, and he really is the only guy you’re adding back into that. Turk Wharton is still hurt. You lose Nic Scourton before the season. There are some teams that even if they don’t have the horses pass-rush wise, the plan feels dynamic. It feels like you can pick on people, either with pressure, with stunts, with simulated, whatever. The pass rush plan, independent of the talent, never felt like they were really able to give teams an edginess with how they attacked them. I think I need to see more of that in addition to Jaelan Phillips, for me to feel like this can be better than something like the 17th-best defense in the league.
Derrik Klassen on what’s keeping him up at night: I just worry that because of the current quarterback play, you’re going to waste a year of an expensive roster with no avenue toward whoever the next quarterback is going to be. And they have some ways that they can get out of this expensive roster. You can get out of the Wharton contract next year. Same thing with Robert Hunt. That’ll clear up somewhere around $30 million. But even in that world, half of that money, at least, is probably going to have to go toward whatever new quarterback you’re about to give some money to, unless they can find some way to maneuver in the draft and go get a guy. And so it just feels like they’ve built up this very expensive roster to be like a 9-win division winner of the NFC South. And if they can’t even accomplish that, you start to spiral about what this team-building has started to look like.

full_text:
Haynes King was excellent in the Hall of Fame Game — his only preseason outing — and it led to him securing a spot on Dave Canales' initial roster. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Following the final preseason game Friday, Dave Canales talked about some of the more intriguing roster decisions the Carolina Panthers had to make before Sunday — all of them on offense.
Canales wondered aloud whether the Panthers would keep three quarterbacks (they did), four running backs (they did, although one’s hurt) and what they might do with a “loaded” tight end room (keep ‘em all!).
Those decisions — in addition to going with 10 offensive linemen — prompted the Panthers to stay lean at wide receiver. That meant the release of veteran David Moore, who’d been with Canales at each of his three NFL stops, and Ja’seem Reed, who led the Panthers with two receiving touchdowns in the preseason.
Moore and linebacker Trevin Wallace were the two biggest names among the cutdown-day casualties, a list that also included safety Isaiah Simmons, a 2020 first-round pick from Clemson.
The Panthers made a trade Sunday to add depth to the defensive line, and — given Dan Morgan’s history — almost certainly will make a couple of waiver claims before Monday’s 1 p.m. deadline.
Meanwhile, a few thoughts on the initial roster:
When the Panthers signed Darren Waller two weeks ago, the prevailing thought was someone would have to go to make room for a player who caught six touchdown passes in nine games for the Miami Dolphins in 2025 following a one-year retirement. Ja’Tavion Sanders, with a skill set similar to Waller’s, was viewed as a trade candidate.
But for now, Waller and Sanders are still around, as are Tommy Tremble, Mitchell Evans and Feleipe Franks. That’s a lot.
Because Waller can line up in the slot, the Panthers can categorize him as a hybrid player. And while Franks is a tight end by title, he made the team because of his special teams ability. Still, it will be interesting to see how the TE room shakes out, especially where Waller is concerned. Waller, who turns 34 the day of the season opener against the Chicago Bears, has been targeted just once in a team drill since arriving.
When Wallace was waived, he became the third player purged from the 2024 draft class, Morgan’s first after succeeding Scott Fitterer as general manager. The other two departees were Day-3 picks (Michael Barrett at least brought the Panthers Mike Jackson in a trade), while Wallace is a third-rounder who started 20 games in his first two seasons.
But the addition of Bobby Okereke made either Wallace or Claudin Cherelus expendable, and the Panthers kept the better special teams player. Several of the remaining members of the seven-player draft class have more to prove, either due to injury (in Jonathon Brooks’ case), inconsistency (Xavier Legette) or both (Sanders).
The team’s area scouts uncovered some undrafted gems in Morgan’s first two years as GM, beginning with ex-Holy Cross wide receiver Jalen Coker and continuing with former Florida State kicker Ryan Fitzgerald and linebacker Bam Martin-Scott, whose hamstring injury landed him on injured reserve with a designation to return.
The Panthers think they might have hit on something with quarterback Haynes King, the undrafted free agent from Georgia Tech who made the team despite missing the final three preseason games with a hamstring injury.
King, the ACC’s Player of the Year in 2025 in his sixth college season, can make plays with his arm and his legs — something Morgan has said he looks for in a backup QB. Kenny Pickett, the QB2 behind Bryce Young, signed a one-year contract. So there’s a path for the 25-year-old King, who’s six months older than Young, to slide into that role in 2027.
The Panthers kept three UDFAs on the initial roster for the third year in a row, with offensive lineman Albert Reese and defensive tackle Aaron Hall joining King on the 53. The 6-foot-7, 325-pound Reese entered Friday’s preseason finale against Houston as one of Pro Football Focus’ top-rated rookies, then struggled against a much shorter Texans edge rusher. But Reese has size and position flexibility, starting games at guard and tackle at Mississippi State.
With Turk Wharton out following neck surgery and Bobby Brown missing time early in camp, the 6-foot-4, 300-pound Hall saw plenty of reps during camp and made the most of them. Hall finished the preseason with five tackles, and shared a sack with Trevis Gipson on Kyle Allen at Buffalo in the second exhibition game.
As mentioned in our last roster projection, the Panthers were interested in adding depth to the interior of the defensive line. Rather than rely on the waiver wire, they traded a sixth-round pick in 2028 for Los Angeles Chargers defensive tackle TeRah Edwards, a 6-foot-2, 305-pounder who was undrafted out of Illinois in 2025. Edwards spent his rookie season on the Chargers’ practice squad and had 10 tackles during preseason games this year.
The Panthers will continue to look for help along both lines, and they’ll need to clear a spot for Okereke and anyone else they bring in. As it stands now, the roster includes 27 offensive players, 23 on defense and three specialists.

full_text:
Jalen Hurts and the Philadelphia Eagles are narrow favorites to win the NFC East. Cooper Neill / Getty Images
Jayden Daniels took the NFL by storm with his Offensive Rookie of the Year campaign that carried the Washington Commanders to 12 wins and the NFC Championship Game — the franchise’s best year since its last Super Bowl win to cap the 1991 season. An elbow injury coupled with natural regression sent Daniels and the Commanders crashing back down to Earth, clearing the lane for the NFC East’s new power, the Philadelphia Eagles, to lead the division.
The Eagles are once again favored to win it with +120 odds at DraftKings that give them a 45 percent implied probability, with the Dallas Cowboys a clear second at +205 and a 32 percent implied probability. That leaves the Commanders with around a 16 percent implied probability at +500, just a hair above the New York Giants at +600 and 14 percent.
We compared those numbers to my model. Here’s a break down of the projections below.
I’m not counting on the Commanders challenging the Eagles or Cowboys for the NFC East crown. The defense needs to take a big step forward after their offseason signings, but I still don’t project them to be an average unit. And while the Cowboys might not either, the Commanders offense isn’t to the same level — and camp reports give me serious doubts they’ll close the gap.
Laremy Tunsil was lost to torn triceps a few weeks ago, and the buzz around camp is that Jayden Daniels has been running for his life. Nicki Jhabvala, who covers the Commanders for The Athletic , described the offensive line as “inoperable” coming out of the team’s joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens. That’s not what you want to hear coming off a season that Daniels wasn’t able to stay healthy.
Perhaps the most concerning factor is Washington’s schedule. The Commanders play the third-toughest schedule, according to my model, while the Cowboys face the eighth and Eagles face the 20th. And it gets tough right off the bat with trips to Philadelphia, Dallas and San Francisco while hosting the Seattle Seahawks, Indianapolis Colts, Giants, Eagles and Los Angeles Rams through the first eight games.
I’m not sure the Commanders are even in the playoff race by Week 10.
A struggling offensive line with an average (at best) defense facing one of the league’s toughest schedules is a recipe for a 7-8 win season. Meanwhile, the Cowboys have an elite offense and the Eagles should have an elite defense. Those units alone should carry those teams to 9-10 wins — or more.
Now, not all hope is lost for Washington fans, as the Eagles and Cowboys combine to win the division about 75 percent of the time. The Commanders come in at 15 percent, and this is the NFL, so anything can happen. But if the offensive line doesn’t improve, it’s hard to see my model being very optimistic about their chances.

full_text:
Tay Martin impressed throughout training camp and the preseason as a receiver and special teams player. Andy Lyons / Getty Images
The Detroit Lions’ 53-man roster is out, and it’s chock-full of surprises and twists.
Five running backs instead of four? Wait, how many receivers? Three tight ends, but which tight ends? Who was the lone UDFA to make the roster? A local product waived at cornerback?
Let’s answer these questions and more, now that the Lions’ 53-man roster is here.
A couple of names jump out. Greg Dortch was a presumed lock when he signed with the Lions in free agency. He felt like a logical replacement for Kalif Raymond, who signed with the Chicago Bears this offseason. He’s younger than Raymond, played for new Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing in Arizona and had what felt like a very good training camp. But the Lions, evidently, believed there were only four receivers worthy of a spot on the 53-man roster. It feels light, but it’s possible there’s some maneuvering left to be done. Tom Kennedy and Dortch were Detroit’s top punt returners, and neither made the roster. A bit puzzling for now, but a reminder that these are just initial rosters.
Early in camp, Nick Whiteside looked like one of the top corners on the roster. Coach Dan Campbell praised him for being fearless when lined up against Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown. He was a menace in one-on-one drills versus receivers and was carrying it over to the preseason. Despite a difficult finish, it felt like Whiteside had done enough to make the roster. He’s subject to waivers, so we’ll see whether he clears and can return on Detroit’s practice squad.
Tyler Conklin felt like a roster lock. He routinely repped as TE3 behind Sam LaPorta and Brock Wright, and he’s a veteran the team signed in free agency this offseason. Again, we’ll have to wait for the dust to settle, but Conklin felt safe. Instead, the Lions go with three TEs — with second-year converted WR Jackson Meeks earning the final spot. Meeks felt like he was on the cusp of a spot, and in the end, he got one.
The inclusion of running back Jabari Small is a bit of a surprise. It felt like the Lions would go with four: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki and Jacob Saylors. Small offers value on special teams, and considering the Lions could be without Pacheco for the opener, maybe they wanted to go heavier at RB.
• Eric O’Neill had himself a camp. He made his presence felt in training camp, performed when given opportunities in the preseason and, against most projections, ends camp with a roster spot. The player out of Rutgers is the only 2026 UDFA to earn a spot on the initial 53-man roster. It felt like he kept showing the coaching staff tools he possessed, and when it was time to translate them to games, he rose to the occasion. At the very least, it felt like O’Neill had done enough to earn a spot on the practice squad, but maybe the Lions felt he put out too much good tape to risk losing him.
• Tay Martin is undoubtedly one of the biggest risers this camp. He beat out a crowded field of receivers and earned the fourth and final spot on Detroit’s initial 53-man roster, behind a trio of starters, St. Brown, Williams and Isaac TeSlaa. Martin is here because of his consistency on special teams, first and foremost. Whenever you asked Campbell or special teams coordinator Dave Fipp about Martin, they praised his daily playmaking on special teams. Martin also proved to be a solid receiving option when the Lions went his way in the preseason. From relative unknown to a roster spot, Martin is one of the better stories we’ve seen this camp.
• Though you expected the Lions to keep Skyler Gill-Howard as a draft pick, the fact he earned his spot makes it all the more satisfying for him and his family. Gill-Howard was one of the most disruptive defensive tackles in the preseason, constantly blowing up double teams and winning with an explosive first step and burst. Though he’s far from a complete player and will need continued patience against the run, Gill-Howard’s profile as a three-tech with pass-rush juice in the interior will get him on the field in certain packages. That’ll play.
• And how about Ahmed Hassanein? You won’t find a player more appreciative of being in this league than Hassanein. He wants nothing more than to be a factor for this defensive line, and after an excellent training camp, Hassanein made the initial roster, after being waived injured around this time last season. It’s a testament to the work he’s put in.
There are 23 offensive players compared with 27 defensive. Some of those spots, such as WR, feel light. Five running backs feels a bit heavy. Will the offensive/defensive split get evened out over the next few days? Certainly possible. It’ll be fascinating to see which releases were a product of roster management more than anything, paving the way for a quick return in some fashion. You see it often with veterans.
Will any of Detroit’s waived players the team hopes will sneak through to the practice squad be claimed? It didn’t happen last year. Will we see the Lions make a claim or two this year and continue to tweak the roster after cutdown day? The Lions kept 53 instead of last year’s 50, so there’s less room to work with, but it they can’t rule it out. The Lions added Tyler Lacy, Tyrus Wheat and Daniel Thomas last year.
As for weak spots, is the combination of Devin White and Malcolm Rodriguez enough to replace Alex Anzalone at linebacker? Is Juice Scruggs capable of holding down the fort at center until Cade Mays returns? Is Blake Miller ready for his close-up? Do the Lions have enough at safety to bridge the gap to the returns of Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph? Will Branch and Joseph look like Branch and Joseph? What if they don’t?
In the end, this roster features top-10 players at various positions across the board. Quarterback, running back, receiver, tight end, tackle, edge, linebacker, etc., but as we saw last year, the top players can only carry this roster so far. The Lions will need contributions (and better health) from the top down to get where they want to go.
Will this roster offer it?

full_text:
Jordan Love leads the promising Pack into the 2026 campaign. John Fisher / Getty Images
It’s about that time — for Lambeau Leaps, for banging the drum all day . The Green Bay Packers are officially back in business from September to January … or perhaps even February.
Green Bay has reached the playoffs in six of Matt LaFleur’s seven seasons on the sideline. Another run is certainly on the table as Jordan Love returns as QB1. Christian Watson, Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden line up out wide, while tight end Tucker Kraft fights his way back from an ACL tear.
The defense added linebacker Zaire Franklin, a 2024 second-team All-Pro, in a trade and brought on the established Javon Hargrave up front. New defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon hangs tight until all-world pocket-wrecker Micah Parsons is healthy again.
The Packers open with three away games through Week 4, but they close out with four of their last five at Lambeau. They also have a pair of Netflix holiday exclusives, both on the road: on Thanksgiving Eve against the stacked Los Angeles Rams, and on Christmas against the hated Chicago Bears. Below, we’re breaking down the viewing options for fans from all over.
Follow the Packers on The Athletic , as well as team beat reporter Matt Schneidman .
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to noted Packers fan Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.
NFL Network has five of the international games, plus a pair of Saturday matchups in Week 16 to be revealed at least two weeks prior to Dec. 26. Those two have 4:30 p.m. and 8 p.m. kickoffs.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or access to NFL+, NFL+ Premium or ESPN Unlimited.

title: Chiefs 53-man roster analysis: 5 things that stood out on cutdown day These were the surprises — and unexpected cuts — from the Chiefs' roster announcement Sunday. Jesse Newell 12
summary: Chiefs 53-man roster analysis: 5 things that stood out on cutdown day These were the surprises — and unexpected cuts — from the Chiefs' roster announcement Sunday. Jesse Newell
full_text:
Running back Emari Demercado, right, was the most surprising cut by the Chiefs on Sunday. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
The Kansas City Chiefs trimmed to the required 53-man roster before Sunday’s deadline … but that doesn’t mean there won’t be changes in the next 24 hours.
Because of their recent run of success, the Chiefs are used to having one of the league’s last waiver priorities. It’s not the case this year.
Because they are coming off a 6-11 season, K.C. ranks ninth in waiver priority if it wants to claim nonveterans who were cut by other teams. That means it’s more likely the Chiefs will make a claim or two this season — especially if they see an opportunity to bolster the depth on their roster.
For now, let’s talk about the current 53, which the team released Sunday afternoon. Here are five things that stood out:
Running back Emari Demercado’s not making the 53-man roster was the biggest news Sunday, and because he’s not a vested veteran, he has been waived and can be claimed by any other team.
Demercado’s roster spot seemed secure before Sunday because of his potential role as a third-down back. He has been one of the team’s top pass protectors out of the backfield, and that would seemingly be an important skill as the team looks to protect quarterback Patrick Mahomes after offseason knee surgery.
The Chiefs view Kenneth Walker III as a potential three-down back , though, and rookie Emmett Johnson made big strides in the final two weeks of camp.
Perhaps both facts — along with a roster crunch at other offensive positions — led the Chiefs to believe others could replace Demercado’s potential contributions.
Second-year left tackle Esa Pole’s getting waived was not expected, but it became at least a possibility once the Chiefs traded for Baltimore Ravens left tackle Diego Pounds on Saturday.
Pole’s stock fell quickly this summer. In June, he was rotating with the first-teamers while battling for the starting right tackle job. Once training camp started, however, Pole only received second-string reps at left tackle, then was passed over in practice by the combination of Jaylon Moore and Kahlil Benson when starting left tackle Josh Simmons was out with injury.
It’s the second straight year the Chiefs surprisingly cut Pole . Last year, he impressed in training camp as an undrafted free agent before getting waived, only to be picked up by the New York Jets. Later in the season, the Jets cut Pole before the Chiefs signed him to their practice squad; he later started four games after the team went through multiple offensive line injuries.
Pounds, an undrafted free agent out of Ole Miss, posted the seventh-highest Pro Football Focus offensive grade among all tackles this preseason with at least 41 snaps. Meanwhile, his pass-blocking grade was second among those 120 qualified tackles.
One of the big questions looming Sunday was whether the Chiefs would keep three or four tight ends.
They went with four. And that meant second-year player Jake Briningstool earned his way.
The 6-foot-6 Briningstool — a 2025 undrafted free agent — had a de facto redshirt season last year while working through a hamstring injury. Once healthy this season, he was most impressive late in training camp, earning some first-string reps while proving to be a big target over the middle and a willing blocker in the run game.
K.C. also had decisions to make regarding keeping extra bodies at quarterback, running back and receiver, so Briningstool’s making the team was no sure thing. His recent uptick was noticeable, though, as he gives the team another developmental player at a position that will likely lose Travis Kelce after 2026.
Special teams coach Dave Toub usually gets a lot of the vote for the final roster spots, and it appears his sway helped return specialist Nikko Remigio earn a place on the initial 53.
Remigio, a 2023 undrafted free agent, is best seen as a special teams security blanket. He’s reliable on catches and isn’t turnover-prone, and that steadiness has helped him secure a spot somewhere on the roster the last four seasons.
His weaknesses are evident, too. Remigio is small at 5-9, 187 pounds, and he also lacks top-end speed, which means he’ll never be a preferred option at receiver. That lack of burst also limits his return upside, as the Chiefs haven’t had a special teams return touchdown since 2020.
The return game needs improvement regardless. Per TruMedia, the Chiefs ranked 25th in expected points added per kickoff return and 21st in EPA on punt returns.
Remigio’s spot meant the Chiefs had to cut someone else. More than likely, that was someone like receiver Andrew Armstrong, a big target at 6-4 who flashed during the final preseason game . He’d have to be considered a top practice-squad candidate should he clear waivers.
The Chiefs cut bigger-name free-agent signings such as Kader Kohou and Kaiir Elam on Sunday. They also cut Melvin Smith, who’d earned some first-string snaps when other players were injured.
A guy who did make it, though? Second-year player Kevin Knowles, a 2025 undrafted free agent who had limited playing time in 13 games for Kansas City last season.
Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has never been afraid to trust undrafted guys once they’ve been in his system a while, and Knowles should help on special teams as well. This was still a surprising addition, especially when it seemed likely Knowles had a good chance to make it back to the practice squad.

full_text:
Aaron Donald agreed on Sunday to return to the Rams, a development that felt both impossible and inevitable. Steph Chambers / Getty Images
LOS ANGELES — For so many seasons, Aaron Donald did the impossible while reminding us that he is inevitable.
The Future Hall of Fame defensive tackle’s decision to come out of retirement this summer, made official on Sunday afternoon, is of the same ethos: It feels impossible. It has felt inevitable.
Donald has been preparing behind the scenes for a return for months, working out at the Rams’ facility and staying in close communication with head coach Sean McVay (who in turn has not been able to keep much of a poker face about the whole thing). Coaches plotted together about how they would utilize him in the event of his return. (Spoiler: a player who already was historically hard to game plan for now has an unpredictable snap count from game to game.)
His eventual return was set in motion by the Rams’ trade in June for another future Hall of Famer, defensive end Myles Garrett. Garrett was a player the franchise had long dreamed about — even inquiring as to the possibility of a trade in 2022, as they discussed how they’d build their Super Bowl-defending roster.
Back then, Donald was also due for the extension that we now know had flexibility built into it on the chance he decided to retire after the 2023 season; there were even reports of a letter of intent to retire that Donald submitted to the Rams that they ultimately tore up.
Pairing Garrett with Donald, organizational leaders knew, would extend the Rams’ window at that time and give them a real shot at repeating as champions. Of course, what actually happened was very different: Garrett was not available; the Rams pursued other options in free agency while extending Donald, quarterback Matthew Stafford and receiver Cooper Kupp; and their 2022 season was a disaster in large part because of injuries. After serving as a bridge for the roster overhaul that followed in 2023, Donald decided he was, in his words, “full.” He stepped away.
But “away” ultimately meant there was a path back. Now, Donald, Garrett, and cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson all count as “offseason acquisitions” on a superteam that still features Stafford, receivers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams and defensive linemen Kobie Turner, Braden Fiske, Byron Young and Poona Ford. That, my friends, is quite a sentence.
It’s so difficult to win a Super Bowl, even as the favorite. Even before Donald’s reinstatement, the Rams had the best odds to do so. Their chances are still just 15.5 percent, according to Austin Mock’s NFL Projection Model ; the Seattle Seahawks and Baltimore Ravens are the next-closest at 7.8 percent and 7.4 percent, respectively.
Last year’s winner, the Seahawks, were given just a 2.1 percent chance of winning, according to the model, while the Bills, Ravens, Chiefs and Eagles ranked among the highest odds (none of them advanced beyond the divisional round, and the Ravens missed the playoffs entirely). In fact, over the last 24 seasons, only four times has the preseason betting favorite (or co-favorite) won the Super Bowl.
All of this to say, the margins for success are slim, and it’s far more likely that things go wrong than right. Careful planning as the Rams have done — turning the sprint-rebuild of 2023 again into a multi-year contender, preserving Stafford’s health and contract, drafting and developing a stellar new core before acquiring resources they ultimately turned into premier players at premium positions (just like in 2021) — only goes so far.
The few players on this Rams roster who have been in the big game before know: It’s the intangible things that also have to go right in November, December, January.
Last time they made a Super Bowl run, it was a different star pass rusher paired with Donald in Von Miller, who sat next to Donald on the plane rides back from road games deep into the season and told him stories about what it was like to win it all. What it felt like to lift the Lombardi Trophy into the lights and confetti on the field afterward, what it felt like to cradle it in his arms in the days and weeks that followed. Garrett does not need any motivation, after the hope-sucking void of many of his years spent in Cleveland with no glimmer of the postseason in sight. But how fitting, now, that Donald will do for Garrett what once helped even the most intrinsically driven player find his extra gear?
That Donald clearly wanted to return before the start of the regular season shows he wants to be a part of that intangible, constant push the team will need to feel every day to reach its championship goals. No surprise there, as that specific type of mental and physical strain is simply Donald’s way of being .
Right now, this is fun. In a few weeks it will be hard.
Maybe the challenge of this is in part why Donald decided to come back. Maybe it’s living in the specific thrill that will come from this team — now one of those “superteams” they make documentaries about — facing these odds and still having a target on its back all season. It will take some luck; any veteran player, coach, executive will tell you that. It will also take some taking-of-chances , another truth everyone in the NFL knows but many will never live by.
There’s a route that the Rams and others have typically built into some of their pass concepts that is called “for the love of the game.” It mostly means that the receiver running it is in charge of executing a deep over route that draws one or more defenders with him, with the intent of clearing out space for other players underneath. Ninety-nine percent of the time he doesn’t get the ball.
But there is that 1 percent …
The Rams lived in those odds once, on a throw from Stafford to Kupp on a “for the love of the game” route that set up a game-winning field goal to win a divisional-round game, then a fateful match against the rival San Francisco 49ers, then an equally fateful march to Super Bowl LVI. That risk was worth everything .
It’s one of the most famous plays in Rams history, of course superseded by Donald closing out the Super Bowl itself with a hit on Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow. It is even rarer than winning a Super Bowl that a defensive player gets to make the game-sealing play.
People often forget about the play before it, during which Donald stopped running back Samaje Perine on third-and-1 and set up his own pass-rush opportunity on fourth down.
Donald, the inevitable force, called his shot at that moment. And now, for the love of the game, for the chance at achieving what in football often feels impossible, he is doing it again.

Dave Helman on what about the Saints most excites him: My enthusiasm is slightly dampened by the Jordyn Tyson situation, but even still, it’s Year 2 of Tyler Shough, and the Saints have done a remarkable job of improving the supporting cast around him. Getting Travis Etienne in there at the price that they did was great. I don’t know if he’s going to change the game for the New Orleans Saints, but it is much better than what they’ve had.
Taliese Fuaga, Brandon (Thorn from “Trench Warfare”) has him ranked 20th among 32 right tackles heading into Year 3. Kelvin Banks comes in at 18th out of 40 left tackles after one season. They paid a premium for David Edwards, but he is a top-10 guard. Erik McCoy, top-five center when healthy, which, please God. And even Cesar Ruiz, who probably gets the least amount of pub among this offensive line, was the ninth-best right guard among 34 ranked. The potential is here for this to be a kick-ass unit.
Derrik Klassen on what he’s watching the first month of the season: I’m watching the defense. We’ve mentioned it a number of times this offseason. Towards the back half of the year, the Saints defense was really good. They were third in EPA per play. When you bring in a new play caller, it (can) take them half the year to really get going. And I think that you really saw Brandon Staley’s defense start to come into its own.
At the same time, I think that this is often a style of defense that is really dependent on what the spine of the defense looks like. You now lose Demario Davis, who was really the heart and soul of this defense through multiple iterations, whether it was with Staley or beforehand with Dennis Allen, and you lose Alontae Taylor, who I think was a pretty good nickel player for them. So these players that were in the middle of your defense and allowing you to do certain things, they’re just going to get different bodies there. And that’s where I think it’s hard to paste on what they did last year to what it might be.
Robert Mays on what’s keeping him up at night: This is a team where you’re looking at the best-case scenario, and it’s so tempting to envision and talk about the best-case scenario. We spent 10 minutes at the beginning discussing the improvements in the supporting cast and the infrastructure around Tyler Shough. What if that just never happens? What if we never get that version of the offense? No Tyson. Erik McCoy’s played 14 games combined in the last two seasons. And I don’t want to face this reality because I loved watching him healthy last year, but Chris Olave has not had a clean bill of health very often throughout his career. And so are we going to be at a place where we’re looking at this offense in Week 12 and there are four or five important pieces missing? You could play this game for every single team. The idea of injuries keeping me up at night. I think it’s a little bit more fitting to have that conversation about this team, considering the point they’re starting from.

summary:

The Jets cut their roster down to 53 on a day when general manager Darren Mougey continued wheeling and dealing. He might not be done just yet.
But for now, the player he added (center Jordan Meredith) will be part of a 53-man roster that both Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn believe is good enough to take a real step forward after a terrible 2025 campaign.

full_text:
The Jets have their initial roster, with changes likely still to come. Margaret Bowles / Getty Images
The Jets cut their roster down to 53 on a day when general manager Darren Mougey continued wheeling and dealing. He might not be done just yet.
But for now, the player he added (center Jordan Meredith) will be part of a 53-man roster that both Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn believe is good enough to take a real step forward after a terrible 2025 campaign.
Here’s a position-by-position look at the initial roster, which is subject to change as the Jets add more players via the waiver wire and/or trades:
Klubnik ultimately “won” the backup job behind Smith, though Bailey Zappe and Brady Cook didn’t exactly provide stiff competition. It’s still possible (if not likely) that the Jets add another quarterback here — who it is will determine if Klubnik maintains his hold on the No. 2 job. I’d be concerned if the Jets actually had to turn to Klubnik early this season in the event that Smith was injured, both for Klubnik’s development and for the short-term performance of the offense. But I do think he’s shown enough to believe in him as a long-term No. 2 option.
Some notable quarterbacks released on and before Sunday include Will Levis, Josh Johnson, Kyle Trask and Jake Browning. Others could be available via trade — particularly from the handful of teams that kept four quarterbacks on their active roster.
Levis is the most intriguing of that group because of his physical and athletic traits, though I’m not sure how much more he does for the offense than Klubnik considering Levis’s turnover tendencies. Levis is subject to waivers though, is only 27 and would cost around $2 million. The Raiders are No. 1 in the waiver order but don’t need another quarterback at the moment.
Breece Hall Braelon Allen Isaiah Davis Kene Nwangwu Andrew Beck
No surprises here. Hall is expected to return for Week 1 and that’s also been the target for Davis, though it’s unclear if he’ll actually be ready to go by then considering he hasn’t practiced in a while. If Davis can’t go, perhaps Mougey will add a running back to the practice squad to call up as needed.
Allen had a nice summer and should finally play the role he was born to play as the Jets’ goal line back.
Beck was a bubble player; ultimately the Jets value his contributions on special teams and as a versatile H-Back-type who can block on offense. Beck surviving the initial cuts means the Jets kept four tight ends and a fullback.
Garrett Wilson Adonai Mitchell Omar Cooper Jr. Isaiah Williams Tim Patrick Arian Smith
Smith was the best case study as to how Mougey and Glenn would approach players they recently drafted. Ex-GM Joe Douglas often hung onto players beyond the point when they deserved to stick around. That’s not to say Smith (a fourth-round pick last year) is entirely in the same bucket — he contributes on special teams, crucial for a fifth receiver — but he has not taken the necessary steps forward as a wide receiver and still has issues with drops, a problem that plagued him in college. Ultimately, the Jets didn’t have any other receivers that seriously pushed him for a spot.
Patrick also didn’t make a huge impact this summer but the Jets value his leadership and ability as a blocker.
Mason Taylor Kenyon Sadiq Jeremy Ruckert Jelani Woods
Sadiq seemed to be making progress in his return from injury lately — it will be interesting to see if he’s ready for Week 1 (and, if he is, whether the Jets activate him that day considering how much time he’s missed). The Jets had big plans for Sadiq coming into the summer, but he missed too much time; offensive coordinator Frank Reich admitted they’ll have to throttle back on those plans a bit. Regardless, this is the best the tight ends room has looked in a long time. Taylor looks ready to take a leap in his second year, Ruckert had his best camp in a Jets uniform and Woods played his way onto the roster with an impressive summer. The Jets might legitimately give snaps to all four of these players (not at the same time, presumably).
Olu Fashanu Armand Membou Joe Tippmann Dylan Parham Josh Myers Jordan Meredith Chukwuma Okorafor Max Mitchell Kohl Levao IR: Anez Cooper
“Trader Darren” was at it again. Last year, Mougey pinpointed a weakness (defensive line) and filled it with two shrewd late-summer trades — for Harrison Phillips and Jowon Briggs. This year, the Jets had an obvious need at center behind Myers. Xavier Newman had a rough summer snapping the ball and was ultimately released on Sunday. Mougey made the trade for Meredith, sending a 2027 sixth-round pick to the Raiders in exchange for the offensive lineman and a future seventh-round pick.
Meredith started 11 games at center last year in Las Vegas — with both Smith and Parham alongside him — and eight at left and right guard in 2024. His best season was in 2024 — his worst might have been at center last year. But he brings valuable versatility, experience snapping to Smith and this should be an environment with the Jets that’s more conducive to offensive-line development than the Las Vegas disaster.
Cooper, the sixth-round pick, was placed on injured reserve with a designation to return. That means, for depth purposes, Meredith is the Jets’ only interior offensive lineman with experience. Levao was a surprise survivor, though the Jets clearly value his versatility — for now, at least, some players won’t stick around if/when Mougey adds via waivers.
T’Vondre Sweat Harrison Phillips David Onyemata Jowon Briggs Darrell Jackson
The Jets finally have depth at defensive tackle. Maybe there’s no star in this group, but Sweat has significant potential if he can stay in shape and stay healthy. The rest of the group slots in well in their roles. Onyemata had a quiet summer but should be fine as a run-stopper, while Jackson was a pleasant surprise as a fourth-round pick who played his way into a rotational role.
David Bailey Kingsley Enagbare Joe Ossai Will McDonald Braiden McGregor PUP: Tyler Baron
Ossai left the preseason finale with a foot injury, the severity of which is unclear. It’s a foursome that complements each other well — Bailey and McDonald as the predominant pass rushers, Enagbare and Ossai as the run stoppers with some pass-rush ability mixed in. Ossai can also slide inside at linebacker as needed. Enagbare actually played well enough during camp to earn the starting job opposite Bailey and he may very well get it.
Remove Ossai and it will put a heavier workload on Bailey and Enagbare — ultimately, McDonald has given no reason to believe he’s anything more than a pass-rush specialist.
Remarkably, McGregor survived cuts for the third straight season even though he’s struggled to produce in the regular season: one sack and two QB hits in 19 games, though he had some moments in training camp and clearly Glenn likes something about his game. Fans might have preferred the late-surging Nate Lynn stick over McGregor, but Lynn ultimately joined the Jets too late in the process. They’ll likely try to keep him on the practice squad.
Demario Davis Jamien Sherwood Kiko Mauigoa Marcelino McCrary-Ball
Mykal Walker was headed toward a roster spot with a solid summer but suffered an injury and was placed on injured reserve without a designation to return, which means he’ll miss the season. Even if Walker had made the team and was healthy, depth at linebacker would still be a real concern. It would be surprising if Mougey didn’t add a linebacker via waivers in the coming days.
Brandon Stephens Azareye’h Thomas Jarvis Brownlee D’Angelo Ponds Nahshon Wright Qwan’Tez Stiggers
It is notable that Ponds wasn’t placed on injured reserve — meaning Glenn’s belief that Ponds could return for Week 1 remains true, or that the rookie at least should be able to return before Week 4 (he would’ve had to miss a minimum of four games on injured reserve). Ponds missed all of camp with a calf strain, so it would be unreasonable to expect him to…

title: How to watch the Philadelphia Eagles in 2026: Channels, streamers for Jalen Hurts' Birds Here's what to know about the Eagles' schedule, with estimated monthly costs for in-market and out-of-market fans. Steven Louis Goldstein 1

full_text:
Jalen Hurts enters 2026 with a 57-25 record as Philly's starting QB. Lauren Leigh Bacho / Getty Images
After decades of ringless futility, the Philadelphia Eagles have become a gold-standard NFL franchise in the Howie Roseman era. They enter the 2026 campaign with eight playoff berths across the last nine years, and a pair of Super Bowl rings to show for it.
Once again, the current Eagles look like one of the conference’s best teams. The offense can set tone and tempo through its ground game — Jalen Hurts under center, Saquon Barkley in the backfield, Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata as anchors up front. When things open up, Hurts has high-upside targets DeVonta Smith, Dallas Goedert and first-round rookie Makai Lemon at his disposal.
Philadelphia boasted the league’s fifth-ranked scoring defense last season. Mad scientist defensive coordinator Vic Fangio still has so much talent to work with this time around. Potential All-Pros abound, including DT Jalen Carter, LB Zack Baun and Cooper DeJean and Quinyon Mitchell in the secondary.
Head coach Nick Sirianni leads a Super Bowl short-lister, with national TV spots throughout the schedule. The Eagles are slated for three primetime night games in the first eight weeks, plus a trip to London in Week 5. They’re also tapped for Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve broadcasts. We’ve compiled this streaming explainer to sort it all out, including options for locals and those far from Philly.
Follow the Birds on The Athletic , and stay up on the beat with senior writer Zach Berman and staff writer Brooks Kubena .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC, and it’s where you can find the Eagles’ Thanksgiving Day rivalry clash against the Dallas Cowboys.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst (and former Eagles antagonist) Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
The Eagles’ lone TNF appearance comes on Christmas Eve, when they host the Houston Texans.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network…

full_text:
Both quarterback Andy Dalton, left, and Will Shipley made the Philadelphia Eagles' initial 53-man roster for 2026. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
The Philadelphia Eagles kept all four quarterbacks on their initial 53-man roster on Sunday. They didn’t keep either international project, either, waiving both Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru.
The roster might change as soon as Monday when waiver claims are processed. It will certainly change in the coming weeks. But the Eagles made their decisions in cutting the depth chart from 91 to 53.
Here is a player-by-player breakdown, with The Athletic ’s Zach Berman breaking down the offense and special teams and Brooks Kubena taking the defense.
Jalen Hurts: Hurts is the franchise quarterback and enters his fifth season as one of the league’s biggest stars, with a Super Bowl MVP on his resume and playoff appearances every year. After the offense’s regression in 2025, the Eagles made their biggest schematic overhaul in Hurts’ time as the starter. He must demonstrate that he can adjust to this offense during the last year of major guaranteed money on his contract.
Andy Dalton: Dalton is in his 16th NFL season and started 173 games between the regular season and postseason. His value at this point is the experience he brings to the meeting room and the field. He also has a background with this offense.
Tanner McKee: McKee spent the offseason in a quarterback competition with Dalton after serving as the No. 2 quarterback last offseason. He struggled to adjust to the scheme and could not separate himself from Dalton. McKee looked like a potential starter as a fill-in quarterback late in the 2024 season. It’s unclear whether Dalton or McKee will be the backup on gamedays.
Cole Payton: A fifth-round pick from North Dakota State, Payton is on the roster as a developmental quarterback. His athleticism is an asset. Payton was limited to 21 preseason snaps on offense. Notably, he played punt coverage on special teams.
Saquon Barkley: If 1,140 rushing yards and seven touchdowns are considered a down year, it’s because Barkley was Offensive Player of the Year in 2024. One noticeable drop: Rushes of 20-plus yards, which declined from 17 to 4 in 2025. Barkley remains the bellcow running back and will run more with the quarterback under center in the Eagles’ wide-zone scheme. The offense needs him to look more like his 2024 self. He could also help in the passing game.
Tank Bigsby: Bigsby emerged as a weapon after arriving in a September trade, averaging 5.9 yards on 58 carries. He is the clear No. 2 back and could also contribute as a change-of-pace option.
Will Shipley: A strong summer for Shipley showed that the third-year running back remains a valued player on the roster. He’s behind Barkley and Bigsby at running back, although Shipley will have a clear special teams role and could take on a larger share of the offense if there’s an injury to Barkley or Bigsby.
DeVonta Smith: Smith is the unquestioned No. 1 receiver after the offseason trade of A.J. Brown. The franchise has long felt he has that ability. Smith topped 1,000 yards in three of the past four seasons, but he’s still waiting for his first Pro Bowl. Look for a sharp jump in volume (he averages 110.8 targets per season) and could leap into the category of the most productive receivers in the NFL.
Dontayvion Wicks: A key offseason acquisition who overlapped with Sean Mannion in Green Bay, Wicks impressed during training camp and has a playing style that Nick Sirianni compares to Keenan Allen.
Makai Lemon: The first-round pick and Biletnikoff Award winner is expected to be an early contributor. Lemon missed considerable time in the spring and summer with hamstring injuries.
Hollywood Brown: The Eagles guaranteed $5 million to Brown, who enters his eighth NFL season. Brown hasn’t approached 1,000 yards since 2021 and fits better as a depth option with experience who can still create separation with his speed and quickness.
Darius Cooper: A training camp standout, Cooper is back for his second season with the Eagles after making the roster as an undrafted rookie in 2025. He profiles as a “dirty work” receiver, although he could graduate to a bigger role on offense if he keeps making plays as he did this summer.
Elijah Moore: Moore developed chemistry with Hurts while Lemon was sidelined and gives the Eagles a proven slot option. The 26-year-old had a 61-catch season in 2024 and topped 40 catches in three of his first four seasons in the NFL.
Dallas Goedert: Goedert returns for a ninth season and could be the No. 2 option in the passing game if he stays healthy. He tied for the NFL lead among tight ends with 11 touchdowns last season.
Johnny Mundt: An under-the-radar veteran signing, Mundt is the No. 2 tight end who will help as a blocker. He could see heavy usage in 12 personnel. A 10-year veteran, Mundt played with Sean Mannion in Los Angeles and Minnesota. He’s never had more than 172 receiving yards in a season.
Eli Stowers: The Eagles selected Stowers in the second round, and it always seemed like a pick with 2027 and beyond in mind, and Stowers did not showcase playmaking skills in the passing game this summer. Unless he sees a spike in his progress behind the scenes, it might be unrealistic to expect much from Stowers this season.
E.J. Jenkins: A surprise inclusion on the 53-man roster, Jenkins has bounced between the practice squad and active roster during the past two seasons. He gives the Eagles depth at a spot where they need it.
Jordan Mailata: Mailata is the franchise left tackle for the Eagles, but he’s still looking for his first Pro Bowl appearance. He’s a key player protecting Jalen Hurts’ blindside and is also a valued voice as a captain for the team.
Landon Dickerson: The Eagles need a healthier version of Dickerson in 2026 after injuries limited him throughout the 2025 season. Dickerson said he’ll reconsider playing through injuries this year. When he’s at his best, he is an All-Pro-caliber left guard.
Cam Jurgens: Jurgens entered last season coming off back surgery, and the injury affected him on the field. Jurgens is healthier this summer, and he’s noticed it with his performance. It’s his fifth NFL season and third season as the starting center. He’s among the NFL’s best when he’s healthy.
Tyler Steen: This is Steen’s second season as the Eagles’ starting right guard. Teammates have praised his summer performance in his fourth season with the Eagles. A strong season could put Steen in line for a big payday this offseason.
Lane Johnson: One of the best players in franchise history, Johnson is back for Year 14 — and likely his last season in the NFL. The Eagles were 8-2 with Johnson last season and 3-4 without him, which demonstrates his value to the team. If he can stay healthy, Johnson could add a sixth All-Pro honor to a potential Hall of Fame career.
Markel Bell: The Eagles took the 6-foot-9, 346-pound Bell in the third round, and he stood out during his first camp with the team. (Literally, and with his play.) Bell could be the swing tackle called upon to step in if there are injuries to Mailata or Johnson. He’s also a candidate to replace Johnson at right tackle after this season.
Fred Johnson: A top reserve tackle the past two seasons who played 1,107 offensive snaps during that period, Johnson has not been able to find a starting job elsewhere. A former Jeff Stoutland project, he competed with Bell for the swing tackle role. He still brings experience to the line.
Drew Kendall: Kendall is likely to be the top reserve interior lineman and can play both center and guard. A fifth-round pick in 2024, he showed strides in his development this summer and helped the Eagles feel better about their depth on the interior.
Willie Lampkin: Lampkin’s impressive training camp and preseason earned him a roster spot. He’s the shortest offensive lineman in the NFL at 5-11, but his balance, strength and movement skills allow him to compensate for his lack of…
